extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, experimentalists, instrument-makers, and Royal Society members
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, constructing, adjusting, and calibrating a clock whose movement descends on an inclined plane, including mechanical layout, balance/equilibration, and procedures to tune its period to 24 hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exterior construction and dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The exterior of this movement or clock is a circular body of 31 inches diameter, consisting of 2 plates measured by the same radius, and fixed in a parallel position to each other by the hoop h, the breadth of which is about an inch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two plates and hoop form the case; anterior plate is inscribed with a horary circle near the edge. The plates are to extend all round beyond the hoop by about a small fraction of an inch and the edges slightly indented so that while the movement descends upon the stage it may turn only, and not slide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dial and index arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Anterior plate towards the edge is inscribed with a horary circle, the divisions of which answer to the hours of a natural day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prominence (hemisphere) with an index (ornamental winged figure) may be used, but any other index may be substituted provided its axis moves freely in the hole H and the lower part preponderates so the index remains pendulous with its point to the vertical hour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage (inclined plane) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage is a straight, even board about 6 feet long, thick enough not to warp with weather or small weight; it is raised at the end S about 10° above the horizon, and the angle of declivity is variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage must be stable so the movement can perform its course; with a 6-foot stage the movement need be replaced at S no oftener than once a week.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall timekeeping principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The movement placed near S will move downward towards E with such slowness as to finish one entire revolution in 24 hours; the hours are shown by the access of the numbers to the suspended, fixed-position index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrary to ordinary clocks, the hour is shown by the dial moving relative to a fixed index. The movement's perpetual descent supplies motive power; no fuse required if properly adjusted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment of rate by stage elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: By a screw inserted in the stage at S, by turning which the stage may be elevated or depressed, the movement will go faster if raised up and slower if let down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the arched screw to set stage elevation (about 10° recommended) and thereby tune speed. If the movement runs too fast/slow, alter stage height rather than immediately changing weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting the dial alignment (horary circle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the horary circle moveable and insert several small bosses or buttons upon its verge so it may be moved right or left with an easy touch until the just time be brought to the suspended index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides fine alignment of indicated time without altering other mechanical settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterpoise P dual role and sizing
rubrics_metrics.description: The weight P has two offices: first, to be a counterpoise to the excess of one section of the body above another; second, to be of force sufficient to put the train into motion so adjusted as may exactly comport with the time assigned for the revolution (once in 24 hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact stating of the intrinsic and potential (by elevation in quadrant) weight/power of P is required so it can serve both roles. If P is too heavy, moderate by screwing down the stage; if too light, compensate by screwing the stage higher. Prefer the heavier extreme (i.e., err on somewhat heavier P) so fewer degrees of extra rise in quadrant are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power modulation by lever elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever the intrinsic weight of P is, its power will be augmented or diminished according to the different degrees of its elevation in the quadrant QT, since PM acts as a lever with fulcrum M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raising P in the quadrant increases effective torque on the train; lowering reduces it to nil at certain positions. Thus potential weight (via elevation) is an important design parameter in addition to mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positioning of great wheel and preservation of P's geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: The great wheel in this case must, with its axis or arbor M, possess the centre of the movement, because this wheel is to carry the weight P by the lever MP, and that weight must always keep equidistant from the centre of the movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures that during revolutions the weight P and great wheel remain without considerable variation in position, avoiding cyclical changes in torque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibration of centre of gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: The inside of the hoop which forms the case is to be loaded with a thin lining of lead as a counterpoise to parts of the train so that the whole body (except P) may rest or ride indifferently on any point; this reducing of the movement to an equilibration of all its parts in the centre M must be performed by trials, i.e. by rasping the lead at CQ as needful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equilibration by trial and rasping is a fine-shop adjustment and should not be difficult to an artificer of ordinary sagacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train gear ratio design
rubrics_metrics.description: The numbers of the teeth on the wheels and pinions are to be so calculated that the motion of the whole train may correspond to the assigned revolution of the body of the movement (once in 24 hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the gear train analogous to a watch but with tooth counts set to produce the slow 24-hour revolution; consider applying a spiral spring to the balance as is usual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of balance and optional spiral spring
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be expedient that a spiral spring be applied to its balance, as is usual in the latter movement; but there is no need of a fuse; the turns of the body as it descends answer the purpose of a string or chain; the counterpoise P serves instead of a perpetual spring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply standard balance-spring practice where appropriate; trust the descent and counterpoise to supply motive restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to test and proportion P experimentally
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the stage about 10° elevation, place the movement, try weights hanging at lever end to see what will stir the train; hold movement with hand such that the level makes about 30° with the perpendicular MT, let movement loose to vibrate on stage; when vibration ceases observe degree of quadrant lever and pulses of the balance to judge proportion of P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If weight lies low (e.g., between 25 and 35 degrees) and beats of the balance are close to due time, P is well proportioned. If too heavy, screw down the stage; if too light, screw stage higher. Prefer a slightly heavy P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding sliding: plate edge indentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Two plates which form the case of the movement are to extend beyond the hoop and the edges of them slightly indented so that while the movement descends upon the stage it may turn only, and not slide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure contact geometry enforces rotation rather than lateral sliding to preserve predictable motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical shop guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Many adjustments (e.g., equili­bration by rasping lead, testing weight P, choosing few degrees P rises beyond necessary) are to be done by trials and artisan judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An artificer of ordinary sagacity will find these adjustments straightforward; perform iterative trials and small material removal rather than large design changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 1: man/horse carrying vs drawing at a pulley
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the difference between what a man or horse can carry and what they can draw up at a pulley.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design controlled trials comparing carrying vs drawing, to quantify mechanical advantage and practical loads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 2: endurance carrying over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the difference in what a man can carry for 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, &c. hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run endurance tests over assigned durations to obtain capacity decay with time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 3: speed under varying burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the difference of speed that a man can make under several burdens within the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify how burden affects travel speed over fixed distances/times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 4: weight of Irish car vs burthen a horse can draw; similar vehicle comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the difference between the weight of a common Irish car and the burthen which a horse can draw upon it; similarly examine a cart for 5 horses and its burthen, a coach with coachman and its burthen, and a pack-saddle/pack-horse with its burthen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare vehicle tare weights to payload capacities across vehicle types to determine efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 5: draught differences between small car and large cart/waggon
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the difference between a horse's draught on a small car and a 5-horse draught on a great cart and 4-wheeled waggon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure required tractive effort for different vehicle/horse combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 6: effect of harness/attachment distance and wheel height
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine differences of horses' draught at several distances from the carriage and upon wheels of several heights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically vary hitch point distance and wheel diameter to determine optimal geometries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 7: optimal wheel spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine at what distance wheels of several heights should stand from each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate wheelbase vs wheel diameter trade-offs for stability and load distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 8: iron vs wooden axles and axle-box friction
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate the difference between iron and wooden axles, and the friction made by them within the boxes of their naves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure frictional losses for axle materials and bearings to recommend materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 9: true reason for dishing out of wheels
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the true reason of the dishing out of wheels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate wheel construction causes (e.g., drying, stresses) and how it affects performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 10: proportional timber in wheel components
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the true proportion of timber which ought to be in the nave, spokes, or rim of any wheel to balance lightness, strength, and uprightness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test cross-sections and proportions to derive construction rules for optimal wheel design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 11: effects of coach hanging height and wheel placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the difference between the high and low hanging of coaches, the distance of the standards, and the difference between the hind and the fore wheels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze suspension geometry and weight distribution to optimize ride and draught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other experiments: pulley-drawn log over level table
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a wooden log (parallelopipedon), test how much weight less than itself, applied to convenient pulleys, will draw the log over a smooth level table of assigned length in assigned time and what weight will draw it faster or slower in assigned proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary applied weight and record speed/time to derive friction/traction relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other experiments: friction of whole side vs keels
rubrics_metrics.description: Test difference in friction of whole side of the log on the plane table and mounting it on two small keels of 1/8 inch thick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare contact area vs keel-mounted friction to quantify rolling vs sliding advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other experiments: segments (imitating dragging wheels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare mounting the log on four thick segments of circles touching the table at 4 points (imitating dragging wheels) and whether it matters if segments are of greater or less circles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess role of contact curvature on draught and friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other experiments: segments vs wheels vs wheelbarrow configurations
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the mounture upon 4 such segments, upon 4 wheels moving distinctly upon their axles, between 2 wheels or 1 segment like a cart, or 1 wheel and 2 segments like a wheel-barrow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify performance differences among mixed rolling/contact schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other experiments: draught on inclinations and surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure differences in draught for the afore‑mentioned mounts on various inclinations of the table upwards and downwards, or on tables covered with a blanket equally extended, or with a paste of clay of certain thickness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test effect of surface compliance and slope on draught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other experiments: wheels vs water draught comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the difference between the tenderest motion upon wheels and the draught through water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare rolling friction to viscous/drag resistance for analogous transport tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid demonstration principle: independent proofs with minimal assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible to demonstrate any of Euclid's propositions independently of the rest, without precedent lemmas or propositions, assuming only basic definitions (angle, triangle, circle, parallels, measure of angle, right angle measure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations should rely on explicit minimal definitions and direct constructions (e.g., using a circle and parallels) so that propositions like the 32d and 47th of the 1st book can be shown without prior results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid proof method for proposition 32
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that an external angle of a triangle equals the two opposite internal ones by drawing a circle with C as center and CD parallel to AB so angles formed by parallels are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use properties of parallels and equal inclinations to a transversal to equate internal and external angles; derive corollaries (sum of triangle angles equals two right angles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid proof method for proposition 47 (Pythagoras)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of squares on the other two sides by constructing squares on each side and comparing excesses via equal triangles and parallelograms in the equal/unequal sides cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle equal and unequal leg cases separately using decompositions into triangles and parallelograms; use superimposition and equality of component figures to establish the equality of squares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion doctrine via definition of similar parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the doctrine of proportionals (permutation, inversion, conversion, composition, division of ratios) can be demonstrated from one definition: that of similar or 'like' parts which are equally contained in their wholes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the single notion of like parts to derive the formal operations on ratios and proportions rather than relying on many lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tides theory: empirical matching and hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for peculiar tides at Tonquin by matching particulars (12-hour flux durations, single high water per 24 hours, intermissions ~14 days apart, 7-day maxima) to moon's position: intermissions near moon's entering Aries and Libra and regulation by moon declination; propose conjecture that increase of waters is proportionate to versed sines of doubled distances of the moon from the equinoctial points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observations, tables of stagnation days, and geometrical construction (figure with perpendicular CD and circles) to compute times and heights of tides with sufficient certainty; seek corroborating navigators' reports from nearby coasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tides caveat: non-proportional rate of sea motion to moon declination
rubrics_metrics.description: Although moon declination regulates these tides, the increase and decrease of the water is by no means proportionate to that of her declination; motion of the sea is scarcely discernible for 3–4 days when moon passes equinoctial points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical models must account for delayed/lagged response and not assume simple proportionality; prefer empirically-tuned functions (e.g., versed sines of doubled distances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting observational astronomy: record precise times and measures
rubrics_metrics.description: For eclipse observations report begin/end times in corrected local time, measure chord(s) of darkened periphery (e.g., 'the chord of the darkened periphery was 11' 25"'), record times when centre emerges and overall duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide precise timed observations and measured obscuration fractions to permit later analysis and corroboration.
